idiom_name: one member function per rule over a token cursor (std::variant tokens, std::string_view lexemes)
implementation_notes: The classic C++ form is a Parser class holding the token buffer and an index, one member function per rule returning a node type, and shared helpers (peek/at/expect/consume) that throw a ParseError carrying a position; from C++11 on, tokens are usually a std::variant or a small struct with a token kind, and lexemes are std::string_view into the source buffer. What replaces the OO parser hierarchy is composition rather than inheritance - rule functions are ordinary members and the AST is built with unique_ptr or an arena - and nothing in the standard library provides the parser itself. Keep this realization when you need exact error positions, custom recovery, arena-friendly allocation and no third-party dependency; choose a combinator variant when the grammar should be declared rather than coded.
pitfalls: std::variant tokens plus std::string_view lexemes are cheap, but the source buffer must outlive every view; a moved or freed buffer leaves dangling views inside the AST.

Throwing ParseError from deep inside rules is the idiomatic error path, yet exceptions must not escape noexcept boundaries and unwinding through the parser loses partial-recovery state; decide early between exceptions and expected-style results.
Rules returning unique_ptr<Expr> move ownership on every reduction; arena allocation or a value-typed AST removes the per-node allocation and the ownership churn.

variants.name: Boost.Spirit X3 grammar (EBNF-style rules)
variants.idiom_name: Boost.Spirit X3 rules built from expression templates (>>, |, *)
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Spirit X3 documents itself as an object-oriented, recursive-descent parser for C++: a rule is an object built from expression templates, so the grammar is written in EBNF-like form (expr = term >> *(('+' >> term) | ('-' >> term));) and compiled by the C++ compiler instead of being expressed as control flow. Attributes bind parse results to types, and the grammar stays free of the generator/lexer split. Prefer it when the grammar should be readable as a grammar and AST binding should be automatic; the costs are heavy template instantiation, long compile times, hard-to-read template diagnostics and a C++14 floor (newer Boost versions move X3 to C++17).
pitfalls: Expression templates make every rule a distinct type: a small mistake in a rule produces a wall of template diagnostics rather than a parse error, so keep rules small and test them in isolation.

Grammar objects are globals with static initialization: a rule that references another before it is defined fails at startup, so declaration order (or x3::rule forward declarations) must be respected.

variants.name: PEGTL PEG combinator grammar
variants.implementation_notes: PEGTL is a header-only parser-combinator library for parsing expression grammars: each rule is a C++ class assembled from rule templates (struct integer : seq<opt<sign>, plus<digit>> {};), the lexer/parser split is normally dropped, and grammar analysis rejects left recursion and other typical PEG mistakes at build time. Actions are attached separately, so the same grammar can drive different ASTs. Choose it over hand-written functions when the grammar should be declared in code, and over Spirit when compile times matter and the PEG semantics (ordered choice, no backtracking into a successful alternative) fit the grammar; the C++17 floor follows the current releases.
pitfalls: PEG ordered choice is not context-free choice: an alternative that succeeds early silently wins, so rule order is part of the grammar and must be tested deliberately.
Deeply nested rules are deeply nested template instantiations: compile times and error message size grow with grammar size, so split large grammars across headers.
